newsitem.title: UK: UK govt no comment on Eurotunnel concession report.
newsitem.headline: UK govt no comment on Eurotunnel concession report.

text.p: Britain's Department of Transport (DOT) and Eurotunnel Plc declined to comment on press reports that the government was considering an extension to the group's Channel Tunnel concession in return for plans to increase rail freight traffic.

The report in Wednesday's Financial Times said John Prescott, deputy prime minister and head of the transport/environment super-ministry, was willing to make a deal if Eurotunnel worked to cut freight traffic from UK roads.
A Eurotunnel spokesman told Reuters it had heard "nothing final" from the French and British governments which met in Paris on Tuesday. The UK DOT also declined to comment.
A DOT spokeswoman said the story had not come from its office and reiterated the UK government's position.

"We are prepared to negotiate constructively but will not be bound by any deadline," she said referring to Eurotunnel's July 10 EGM when shareholders will vote on the rescue plan to restructure nearly nine billion pounds in debt.

Eurotunnel has asked to government to extend its concession to 999 years, up from 65 years. But it concedes that any improvement to the term is better than nothing and is sure to strengthen its hand in getting the debt plan approved.

The DOT said Tuesday's meetings between the French and UK governments had concluded without a firm resolution being reached on the issue. The DOT spokeswoman said further talks were planned but gave no new starting date.
Eurotunnel said on Wednesday it would be willing to take any steps to increase traffic through the tunnel and repeated its view that a concession extension is key to clinching shareholder backing.
The plans have come under strong attack from French shareholders in particular in recent days. They now claim they have enough support for a blocking minority.
